blocks.text: Sequence packing combines several shorter training examples into a single, longer sequence, rather than padding each short example out to the batch maximum length individually, reducing the amount of wasted computation spent processing padding tokens.

It is a training efficiency technique that becomes increasingly valuable as a dataset contains a wide range of example lengths, and it connects directly to the tokenization and loss masking concepts covered in the previous topic of this module.
1. The Wasted Space Problem
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448360196-86118284.png

When examples in a dataset vary widely in length, padding every example in a batch up to the length of the longest one means a lot of the sequence for shorter examples ends up filled with padding tokens, tokens the model spends compute processing without gaining any useful training signal from.
At scale, across millions of training steps, this wasted compute adds up to a real, measurable cost in training time and money.
2. What Sequence Packing Does
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471809064-850098206.png

Instead of padding each short example individually, sequence packing concatenates several examples together into one longer sequence that fills the available length far more densely, dramatically reducing the proportion of padding tokens in each batch.
3. The Role of a Separator or Boundary Token

blocks.alt: The Role of a Separator or Boundary Token
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471809066-510477868.png

Since packed sequences contain multiple distinct examples back to back, a special boundary token, or the natural end of sequence token, marks exactly where one example ends and the next begins, information the training process needs to correctly handle attention and loss for each individual example.
4. Preventing Cross-Example Attention Leakage
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471809066-745618689.png

A packed sequence risks a subtle problem, if left unaddressed, the attention mechanism, covered earlier in the Foundation Models module, could let tokens from one packed example attend to tokens from a completely unrelated example sitting right next to it in the same sequence.

Careful implementations use an attention mask specifically designed to prevent this leakage, ensuring each example only attends to its own tokens even though several examples physically share one sequence.

blocks.title: This is the technical detail that makes packing safe
blocks.content: Sequence packing without a correctly constructed cross-example attention mask can quietly corrupt training, since the model would learn spurious relationships between unrelated packed examples.

blocks.text: 5. Efficiency Gains From Packing
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471809067-781279558.png

The efficiency gain from packing comes directly from reducing wasted padding, fewer total batches are needed to get through the same number of real training tokens, which translates into faster training and lower compute cost for the same amount of actual learning signal.

blocks.text: 6. When Packing Is Worth the Complexity

blocks.alt: When Packing Is Worth the Complexity
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471809067-748679732.png

Packing delivers the most benefit when a dataset has a wide range of example lengths, many short examples mixed with a few long ones, since that is exactly the situation where naive padding wastes the most compute.
For a dataset where every example is already roughly the same length, packing adds implementation complexity for comparatively little efficiency gain.
7. Packing and Loss Masking Together
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471809067-807873931.png

Just as the previous Tokenization Pipeline topic covered masking loss to the completion portion of a single example, a packed sequence needs a per-example loss mask, correctly tracking which tokens belong to which original example, so loss is computed correctly for each one independently within the shared sequence.

code.content:
# A simplified packing concept, conceptually
packed_sequence = example_a.tokens + example_b.tokens + example_c.tokens
packed_labels = example_a.labels + example_b.labels + example_c.labels
# Each example's attention mask still isolates it from the others
packed_attention_mask = build_block_diagonal_mask([
    len(example_a.tokens), len(example_b.tokens), len(example_c.tokens)
])

blocks.text: 8. Tradeoffs and Risks of Packing

Packing adds real implementation complexity, correctly building the cross-example attention mask and per-example loss mask is not trivial, and a bug in either can quietly degrade training without an obvious error message, which is why many teams start without packing and adopt it deliberately once training efficiency becomes a real bottleneck.
9. Where This Fits Relative to Training Infrastructure

Sequence packing is one of several training efficiency techniques covered more broadly in the Training Infrastructure module later in this course, and it is worth understanding as a dataset level decision even before reaching that infrastructure focused material.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning on a dataset of short customer support replies mixed with occasional long, detailed technical explanations notices their training runs spend a large share of compute processing padding, since most batches contain a long example forcing every other example in that batch to pad out to match it.

After implementing sequence packing with correctly isolated attention and loss masks, they see a meaningful reduction in training time for the same number of epochs over the same dataset, confirming the padding overhead really was the bottleneck they suspected.
Common Mistakes

items: Packing sequences without a correctly isolated attention mask, letting unrelated examples attend to each other
Forgetting to track per-example loss masks correctly within a packed sequence
Adopting packing for a dataset where example lengths are already fairly uniform, adding complexity for little benefit
Assuming packing is always worth the implementation effort without first measuring how much padding overhead actually exists

blocks.text: Practice

Take the length distribution of a dataset you have access to, or imagine one with a realistic mix of short and long examples, and estimate roughly what fraction of a fixed batch length would be wasted on padding without packing, versus how densely packing could fill that same space.
Key Takeaway

Sequence packing combines multiple training examples into one dense sequence to reduce wasted padding compute, and while it delivers real efficiency gains for datasets with widely varying example lengths, it requires carefully constructed cross-example attention and loss masks to avoid quietly corrupting training in the process.
